body.text: It wasn’t easy to get close to Stephen Sondheim. The composer Mary Rodgers said, “If you walk into a room he’ll ignore you. And if you ignore him, then he’ll come over and say hello. It’s like some goddam cat!” Even if Sondheim did come over, you had to be careful what you said. He didn’t do small talk and, according to the actor Elaine Stritch, “When you say something personal to Steve, he says ‘Taxi!’”

Perhaps it helped Daniel Okrent that he never met the subject of his compulsively readable new book, Stephen Sondheim: Art Isn’t Easy, because the author gets closer to the composer and lyricist than any previous biographer. He has more to go on: letters to collaborators, a lengthy oral history (kept private until after Sondheim’s death in 2021 at the age of ninety-one) and interviews with multiple friends. What emerges is a remarkably complex man: brilliant, private, irascible, addicted, hypersensitive and emotional. We read about John Weidman working with Sondheim on Pacific Overtures in the mid 1970s. The composer had asked the writer over to play him “Someone in a Tree,” but began to cry before his hands even touched the keyboard. He was, said Weidman, “completely undone” by his own song.

Because Sondheim is now generally reckoned the most important creator of musical theatre in the second half of the twentieth century, it comes as a shock to realise that in 1970, aged forty, “his entire body of recorded music consisted of twenty-eight songs from the cast albums of A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum and Anyone Can Whistle,” the former a hit, the latter a flop. He was famous for his lyrics in Bernstein’s West Side Story and Jule Styne’s Gypsy, and that facility for writing brilliant words would dog him through his career. Even after the successes of the 1970s — Company, Follies (despite a disappointing opening run) and A Little Night Music — he was still, in the minds of many critics, a lyricist who also wrote music.

He wasn’t alone, of course. Cole Porter’s lyrics (which Sondheim admired) often seemed to take precedence over his music, and Noël Coward’s (which Sondheim “cordially but intensely” disliked) frequently eclipsed his music. But there was a further charge that never quite went away, and irritated Sondheim his whole life, namely that his tunes were not “hummable.”

What did that even mean? The tunes were certainly catchy — my own head has been full of Sondheim earworms during and after reading Okrent’s book — but perhaps there was something about the closeness of Sondheim’s words and music that gave the music a certain utilitarian nature; minus his lyrics, his melodies don’t always make sense. The words not only articulate the tunes, but they also explain them.

From the start, words and music were inseparable in Sondheim’s art. When his parents’ marriage ended, the young “Stevie” was taken under the wing of Oscar Hammerstein II, perhaps the most successful Broadway lyricist of the twentieth century, his credits stretching from Show Boat (in 1927 with Jerome Kern) to The Sound of Music (in 1959 with Richard Rodgers). Sondheim was in his thrall, famously insisting that had Hammerstein been a geologist, he would have become one too. Though later not uncritical of Hammerstein’s lyrics, the young man began as an imitator, until his mentor upbraided him for writing about “nature and things like that.” He gave the boy important advice: “Write what you believe and you’ll be 99 per cent ahead of the game.” It’s far better advice for an aspiring writer than “Write what you know” because it prioritises imagination.

If words fascinated Sondheim, music obsessed him, and here his most important role model was his teacher at Williams College, Robert Barrow (Sondheim used the geologist line about him too). Barrow played his class Debussy’s La Mer: “Anybody here hear the sea?” he asked. “Well, even if you do, that’s not what it’s about. What the piece is about is the whole tone scale.” Sondheim said he “fell in love” because Barrow had “made it clear that music is a thought-out process, that it is a craft, not inspiration.” Perhaps it was inevitable that, after Barrow, Sondheim should have ended up working with the arch-modernist, Milton Babbitt, who taught him about “long-line form” and building a whole musical work from a handful of notes.

Sondheim’s brilliance was allied to a careful application of all these lessons. You feel he took Babbitt’s advice about “long-line form” and applied it to his lyrics, which always go forward, always advancing the story; and Hammerstein’s advice about writing what he believed is applied to the music, which always served the drama. It wasn’t just that the words explained the tunes, but a song’s situation in the show generally accounted for both words and music. Sondheim’s songs emerge from characters, from their personalities and the situations in which they find themselves. He couldn’t just write a love song. He needed to know who was loving whom and why.

On the page, the ideas for his shows (which were almost never his) were often unpromising. Company, for example, was the distillation of eleven one-act plays by George Furth, a man who, in Okrent’s words, was “about as musical as a sofa.” But Sondheim and his “enthusiasm” — collaborator Harold Prince — spotted the potential in a blank central character, Bobby, surrounded by the company of his friends and relations, and the result was structurally groundbreaking. Alan Jay Lerner (My Fair Lady, Brigadoon) arrived home from having seen it and broke down in tears, telling his wife, “My way of writing musicals is over.”

But there was something else about Company. Its success made Sondheim famous on a whole new level and now there were people — not just his friends and colleagues, but members of the public — who wanted to know how autobiographical Company was. Was Sondheim Bobby? Remember, the book of the show was not by Sondheim, but those songs, embodying the drama, conveying the story, displaying the character, linked their composer to his creation as though the whole thing was about him. In Bobby’s big number “Being Alive” he sings (to the same handful of notes that had called his name at the start of the show):
Somebody crowd me with love Somebody force me to care Somebody let come through I’ll always be there As frightened as you, to help us survive Being alive.

You don’t need to be a psychoanalyst (Okrent, more than once, refuses the tag) to wonder if this blank man, alienated yet desperate for love, is self-portraiture. This was not the first time the question had been posed, and it certainly wouldn’t be the last. It goes back at least as far as the title song of Anyone Can Whistle, in which the idealistic Fay Apple sings that while whistling might be easy for some it doesn’t come easily to her.
Anyone can whistle That’s what they say — Easy Anyone can whistle Any old day — Easy It’s all so simple Relax, let go, let fly So someone tell me why Can’t I?

You can hear Sondheim himself sing this song on a demo made in 1963. He’s not a great singer — his pitch tends to waver — but all his demo recordings bring insights to the songs. Perhaps this one brings more. Okrent detects a slight catch in the singer’s voice, “almost imperceptibly cracking on the final note,” and so do I. •
Stephen Sondheim: Art Isn’t Easy By Daniel Okrent | Yale University Press | $39.95 | 320 pages
